summary: EarthEcho: The Earth Information Jukebox is a browser-based project that makes NASA Earth imagery more accessible by turning visual patterns into sound. It is designed to help people explore information about our planet through both sight and hearing. The prototype scans an Earth image using a visible cursor and converts image features into musical tones. As the scan progresses, users can hear changes in the generated sounds and follow the visual movement on the screen. Playback controls allow users to start, pause, and explore the experience at their own pace. Plain-language explanations describe how image features are connected to the sounds, helping users understand the process rather than treating it as a mysterious effect. EarthEcho focuses on transparency, accessibility, and interactive learning. By combining imagery, sound, and clear explanations, the project offers another way to engage with Earth observation data and encourages curiosity about environmental patterns and the changing planet.
details: EarthEcho is a browser-based prototype that transforms visual patterns in Earth imagery into interactive sound. Designed for The Earth Information Jukebox challenge, it aims to help users explore NASA Earth Information Center visualizations through hearing as well as sight. The project combines a visible scanning cursor, generated tones, playback controls, and plainlanguage explanations. Its central principle is transparency: users should understand which image feature produces each sound and what that sound cannot establish. The prototype code has been generated and packaged. Its browser performance, audio synchronization, and accessibility have not yet been independently tested. A verified NASA visualization still needs to replace the synthetic teaching image before the final NASA-based demonstration. 1. Problem and intended users EarthEcho explores how sound can provide an additional way to investigate an Earth visualization. Rather than simply adding background music, it connects audio directly to identifiable image features. The intended users include: Students exploring Earth imagery. Teachers developing interactive demonstrations. Visitors to science exhibitions and public displays. People interested in alternative ways to explore visual information. The intended benefit is greater engagement and understanding of the selected visualization. These benefits remain project goals until evaluated with users. The project does not claim that its accessibility or educational effectiveness has already been validated. 2. Proposed solution EarthEcho provides a guided exploration sequence: 1. Choose an image and inspect its source information. 2. Hear calibration sounds explaining the mapping. 3. Play a le-to-right scan of the image. 4. Follow the cursor while listening to the corresponding tones. 5. Pause, adjust speed, or inspect an individual column. 6. Read the mapping explanation and scientific limitations. For the initial NASA-based version, the scope is deliberately limited to one verified visualization and one consistent sound mapping. 3. How the sonification worksThe prototype divides the displayed image into 96 columns and eight horizontal bands. Image feature Audio representation Horizontal position Playback order, from le to right Vertical band Pitch, with higher image bands producing higher notes Mean displayed RGB brightness Tone strength Selected column The region inspected or played Scan duration The speed of exploration For each analysis cell, the application calculates: Here, is the number of pixels in the cell, and the red, green, and blue channel values range from 0 to 255. The result is a normalized summary of displayed RGB brightness. Each horizontal band uses a fixed pitch. The application converts the brightness summary into tone amplitude, with an additional user-controlled master volume. This is a designed translation of image features—not a reconstruction of physical sound or an environmental measurement. 4. Main prototype features The generated application code includes: Feature Purpose Local image import Load a PNG, JPEG, or WebP image Synthetic teaching pattern Demonstrate the system without misrepresenting it as NASA data Calibration sounds Explain brightness and pitch before playback Scanning cursor Connect the audio to the current image location Playback controls Play, pause, and restart exploration Adjustable scan duration Let users explore at different speeds Volume control Support user-controlled listening levels Column inspection Examine a selected part of the image Source metadata fields Record the title, source, credit, and observation period Image-description field Provide a written description of the selected visualization Feature export Download the calculated grid and entered metadata Built-in feature tests Check defined image-processing behaviors These are features present in the generated source code, not independently verified performance results. 5. Technical implementationThe proposed implementation uses a small, static web application. Component Role HTML Page structure and controls CSS Layout and visual styling Component Role JavaScript Interaction, processing, and playback logic Canvas Image display and pixel analysis Web Audio API Tone generation and audio scheduling JSON Metadata and feature-grid export The processing sequence is: Imported image ↓ Documented image preparation ↓ Displayed RGB feature extraction ↓ 96-column × 8-band feature grid ↓ Playback position ↓ Generated tones + visible cursor ↓ User exploration and explanation The generated version does not require an application backend, user accounts, or a live NASA data feed. 6. NASA data and visualization contribution NASAʼs contribution should be the Earth visualization that users explore. EarthEcho adds the interactive audio layer; it does not create new Earth observations. Before the final demonstration, the team must select and document a verified NASA Earth Information Center resource, including: Exact visualization title. Original source page. Observation period. Required credit and attribution. Any cropping, resizing, or other preparation. A description of the image and its relevant limitations. No NASA image is currently bundled with the generated prototype. The starter pattern is synthetic and must remain clearly labeled as such. The final demo should visibly connect the selected NASA resource, the user experience, and the resulting project, as requested by the supplied guide. [36]7. Creativity and distinguishing approach EarthEchoʼs proposed creative emphasis is not simply turning an image into music. It is making that translation inspectable. The design combines: Calibration before exploration. A visible connection between scan position and sound. User-controlled pacing. Individual-column inspection. Source attribution alongside the experience. Clear separation between visual features and scientific quantities. The project does not claim to have invented sonification. Its focus is an understandable, reproducible interaction built around a NASA visualization. 8. Scientific validity and limitations The project distinguishes three separate claims: Level Appropriate claim Source The image comes from the cited visualization Processing The algorithm calculates a documented displayed-image feature Interpretation The sound offers a way to explore that image’s visual patterns Important limitations include: Displayed RGB brightness is not calibrated radiance. Color palettes and contrast settings affect the output. Labels, legends, and borders can introduce unwanted sounds. Resizing and image compression can change feature values. Averaging can reduce the influence of small bright features. Different image renderings cannot automatically support scientific comparisons. Audio patterns do not establish population, electricity consumption, environmental risk, or causation. Accordingly, EarthEcho makes no “100% accuracy,” prediction, or scientific-diagnostic claim. 9. Testing and evaluation planImage-processing tests The generated application includes tests for: 1. A black image producing zero brightness values. 2. A white image producing maximum brightness values. 3. A uniform gray image producing the expected normalized value. 4. A bright patch appearing in the correct analysis cell. 5. Repeated processing producing identical output. The tests must be executed and their actual results recorded. Playback and interaction tests The next evaluation stage should check: Cursor-to-audio synchronization. Play, pause, restart, and column selection. Audio levels and clipping. Behavior across the browsers and devices used for the demo. Keyboard-only operation. Error handling for unsupported or missing images. User evaluation Participants should attempt to: Identify which of two regions produces the stronger tone. Associate higher and lower pitches with the correct image bands. Pause and inspect a selected column. Explain what tone strength represents. Identify what the audio cannot establish. These tasks would provide evidence about mapping comprehension rather than relying on general claims that the experience is intuitive. 10. Expected impact and development statusEarthEchoʼs intended outcome is a small educational experience that encourages curiosity while keeping its mapping and limitations visible. Potential settings include classroom demonstrations, science exhibitions, and public Earth-information displays. Project element Current status Project concept and technical specification Created Browser application source package Generated Project element Current status Project PDF and seven-slide presentation Created Verified NASA asset integration Pending Browser execution and performance verification Pending Audio synchronization measurements Pending User and accessibility evaluation Pending Public deployment Not completed The immediate milestone is one verified NASA visualization, one tested playback experience, and a demonstration supported by actual results. 11. Submission presentation The supplied guide evaluates projects under Impact, Creativity, Validity, Relevance, and Presentation. It requires either a video of no more than 30 seconds or a slide deck of no more than seven slides, including title and introduction slides. The demo must be externally hosted and publicly accessible; slides and submission materials must be in English, with English subtitles required for non-English video narration. [36] The final submission must include the actual team name and members, selected challenge, working project demonstration, user experience, and NASAʼs contribution. Until the missing source, testing, identity, and public-link details are completed, EarthEcho should be presented as a prototype under development rather than a fully validated solution.
